Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'inspect' returns the accessibility tree of the front app (what a screen reader reads, which can differ from what is drawn) as JSON — per element: type, label, value, frame [x,y,width,height] in device points from the top-left, traits the type does not imply, enabled only when false, children. Prefer it to 'screenshot' to find what to tap (tap a frame's center), read text, or check a control's state or value; use 'screenshot' for layout, color, and images. Default: the whole visible tree; x/y: the element under that point with its descendants (a point between controls hits their container); marker: the first element whose label (or match_key) contains that text. Hidden, off-screen, and illegibly small elements are omitted and counted, and text longer than its area shows is cut and ends with ... (occlusion and transparency are not detected); a tree over the size cap loses its deepest levels first and says so — narrow with x/y or marker; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

marker.description: For 'inspect': return only the first element (tree order, with its descendants) whose match_key attribute contains this case-sensitive substring. Omit for the whole tree, or pass x/y instead for the element under a point.

match_key.description: For 'inspect' with 'marker': the attribute to match — label (default), value, or role (the element type).

# rbtree-lab: project rules

## Commands
- Build & unit tests: `make test`
- Sanitizers: `make asan`   Valgrind: `make memcheck`
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.

## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
  leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
  looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.

## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.

## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
  approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".

## Code map
- `src/rbtree.c` — the whole implementation. Opaque `struct rbtree` and the
  node struct live here, invisible to tests.
- All allocation goes through `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` in that file, never
  malloc/free directly. That seam is what HW2 swaps out.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit and table-driven case tests.
- `tests/fuzz.c` — random ops vs. a reference model; op count is `argv[1]`.

## Ownership
Three separately-owned things per node: the node, the tree's private key
copy, and the caller's `void *value`.
- rb_insert returns 0 -> tree owns value. Returns -1 -> caller still owns it.
- Overwrite frees the OLD value via value_free first.
- Rotations change topology only, never ownership.

## Environment
`make memcheck` cannot run on this Mac: no valgrind on Apple Silicon, and
ASan on macOS has no LeakSanitizer. Leak checking needs a Linux machine.
Never report memcheck as passing here.

## Status
M1 steps 1-10 done: full red-black insert. rotate_left/rotate_right own the
t->root update. insert_fixup handles red-uncle (recolor+climb) and
black-uncle (1-2 rotations) with mirrors. rb_validate checks all 5 rules +
parent links + count; failure codes 1-7 name the broken rule.
Still stubs: rb_foreach (M1), rb_delete (M2). Fuzzer is a stub.
Next: rb_foreach (in-order, recursive), then the fuzzer (inserts/finds vs a
sorted-array reference model, validate every 100 ops).

content.text:
Review done. Build is green under ASan/UBSan (`make test`, `make asan`), and I traced the code by hand rather than trusting that. Here's what I found, worst first.

## Confirmed bug

**1. Overwrite with the same value pointer → double free.** [src/rbtree.c:282](src/rbtree.c:282)–[285](src/rbtree.c:285)

The overwrite path calls `value_free(cur->value)` and then stores `value`. If the caller passes the pointer the tree already holds, you free it and then keep the dangling pointer. `rb_destroy` frees it a second time. I proved it under ASan with a 6-line program (`rb_create(free)`, insert `p` under `"k"` twice, destroy):

```
AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free ... destroy_subtree rbtree.c:438
freed by ... rb_insert rbtree.c:283
```

Fair nuance: after the first insert the tree owns `p`, so passing it again is the caller handing over something they don't own. Under a strict reading of the header, that's caller error. A kernel reviewer flags it anyway because the guard is one comparison and the failure mode is silent memory corruption, not an error code.

## Coverage gaps (the allocation question)

**2. Every allocation *is* NULL-checked — but nothing proves the failure paths work.**

- [src/rbtree.c:74](src/rbtree.c:74) — node struct alloc, checked.
- [src/rbtree.c:80](src/rbtree.c:80)–[94](src/rbtree.c:94) — key alloc, `goto fail` frees the struct. `n->key` is NULL there, `rb_free(n)` touches only the struct, `value` is never stored. Correct by inspection.
- [src/rbtree.c:294](src/rbtree.c:294)–[297](src/rbtree.c:297) — `rb_insert` returns −1 before touching `t->root`, `count`, or any link. "Tree unchanged" holds by inspection.
- [src/rbtree.c:259](src/rbtree.c:259) — `rb_create`, checked.

None of those branches ever execute in the test suite. The repo's own CLAUDE.md rule ("NULL return must leave the tree unchanged") is asserted, not tested. `rb_live_allocs` is already the seam you'd hang a "fail the Nth allocation" knob on.

**3. Test code has unchecked allocations.** [tests/test_rbtree.c:97](tests/test_rbtree.c:97)–[99](tests/test_rbtree.c:99) (`first`/`second` dereferenced with no NULL check), [:128](tests/test_rbtree.c:128) (`v`), and every `rb_create` except the one at [:47](tests/test_rbtree.c:47) — lines [65](tests/test_rbtree.c:65), [95](tests/test_rbtree.c:95), [122](tests/test_rbtree.c:122), [145](tests/test_rbtree.c:145), [208](tests/test_rbtree.c:208), [219](tests/test_rbtree.c:219), [232](tests/test_rbtree.c:232), [243](tests/test_rbtree.c:243), [255](tests/test_rbtree.c:255), [267](tests/test_rbtree.c:267), [299](tests/test_rbtree.c:299). Harmless today. Once HW2 swaps in a fault-injecting `rb_malloc`, a NULL from `rb_create` becomes a segfault in the test binary instead of a clean FAIL line.

## rb_destroy: can it miss a subtree?

No. Reasoning:

- [rotate_left](src/rbtree.c:144) and [rotate_right](src/rbtree.c:167) both reattach the moved middle child (`b`) before anything else and update `t->root` when `x` had no parent. All four call sites in `insert_fixup` ([221](src/rbtree.c:221), [229](src/rbtree.c:229), [243](src/rbtree.c:243), [249](src/rbtree.c:249)) satisfy the "`y` is non-NULL" precondition.
- [destroy_subtree](src/rbtree.c:431) is post-order from `t->root`. The only way it misses a node is if a node is unreachable from the root — and the tests would catch that: `rb_validate`'s count check ([423](src/rbtree.c:423)) runs after every insert, and `expect_clean` demands 0 live blocks after 1000-key ascending and 2000-key random stress.
- [insert_fixup:204](src/rbtree.c:204) — `g = p->parent` is safe because `p` is red ⇒ `p` is not the root ⇒ `g` exists. That depends on the root always being black on entry, which [line 254](src/rbtree.c:254) guarantees unconditionally after every insert.

## Hardening / consistency (low)

**4. `value_free` is called on NULL values.** [src/rbtree.c:102](src/rbtree.c:102)–[104](src/rbtree.c:104) and [:282](src/rbtree.c:282)–[284](src/rbtree.c:284). Fine for `free`; a user callback that doesn't tolerate NULL crashes. Tests never hit this because they only combine NULL values with a NULL `value_free`. Pick a policy and write it down.

**5. NULL handling is inconsistent inside the file.** `rb_size` ([337](src/rbtree.c:337)) and `rb_destroy` ([443](src/rbtree.c:443)) guard `t == NULL`; `rb_insert` ([272](src/rbtree.c:272)), `rb_find` ([315](src/rbtree.c:315)), `rb_validate` ([406](src/rbtree.c:406)) don't. A NULL `key` crashes in `strcmp` ([278](src/rbtree.c:278), [319](src/rbtree.c:319)) or `strlen` ([78](src/rbtree.c:78)). The header only promises NULL-safety for `rb_destroy`, so this is contract-compliant — but decide deliberately rather than by accident.

## Nits

- [src/rbtree.c:128](src/rbtree.c:128) — `bool` with no `<stdbool.h>`. Only compiles because `-std=c23` makes `bool` a keyword. A grader's gcc older than 13 has no `-std=c23` at all and this won't build. Portability, not memory.
- [src/rbtree.c:23](src/rbtree.c:23) — the comment reads backwards ("still want to allocate it" on the NULL branch).
- [tests/test_rbtree.c:63](tests/test_rbtree.c:63) — `int values[7]` is hard-coded while `n` is computed from `keys`. Add a key and you get an out-of-bounds read.
- [.gitignore](.gitignore) — `transcripts/` is now ignored, and `git ls-files transcripts` is empty. The spec lists raw `.jsonl` transcripts as a required deliverable. Not memory, but it's in the diff and it affects the grade if they're supposed to ship in the repo.

Nothing fixed, per your ask. The PoC program is in the scratchpad, not the project.

Three things in order: the double-free guard, the `.gitignore`, then the M2 delete tests. I'll show each diff and run the suite before moving on.

## Step 1 — the double-free guard

The fix is one condition: only call `value_free` on the old value if it's a *different* pointer from the new one. If the caller hands back the pointer the tree already holds, there is nothing to free and the assignment is a no-op.

The alternative was to leave the code alone and document "never re-insert a pointer the tree owns" as a caller rule. I'm going with the guard because it costs one comparison and turns silent heap corruption into a harmless no-op. That's the better trade for a library.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

### Phase 2: Design
Goal: Design an implementation approach.

Launch Plan agent(s) to design the implementation based on the user's intent and your exploration results from Phase 1.

You can launch up to 1 agent(s) in parallel.

**Guidelines:**
- **Default**: Launch at least 1 Plan agent for most tasks - it helps validate your understanding and consider alternatives
- **Skip agents**: Only for truly trivial tasks (typo fixes, single-line changes, simple renames)

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request

Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).

- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number

- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.

Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

recheck two levels up. **No pointers move.** This can repeat — the violation just relocates
  upward; it is NOT guaranteed to finish in one pass.
- Key fact: **on the very first iteration of the fixup loop, a black uncle is always NIL** (a real
  black-with-subtrees uncle literally cannot occur yet — proven by a black-height counting
  argument). Rotation cases with substantial uncles only show up after the loop has already
  climbed once — meaning hand-testing with 5 keys will never exercise them; you need real
  volume (fuzzing) to hit rotation cases.
- When uncle is black: recoloring can't help. Need 1–2 rotations (zig-zag "kink" needs 2: one to
  straighten the shape, one to do the real repair + color swap). **Insert fixup never needs more
  than 2 rotations, total.**
- **Classic bug:** after a rotation moves the root to a new node, if your fixup only patches
  parent/child pointers and never updates `t->root`, `rb_find` starts silently searching a subtree
  and `rb_validate` will happily certify the (wrong) subtree as legal. Write a **stale-root
  regression test** the same day you write rotations.

**Deletion** — the unpleasant direction; damage is a *global count mismatch*, not a local violation.
- Removing a **red leaf** is free (no invariant impact).
- A node with **two children**: hoist the in-order successor's key+value into the doomed node's
  slot, then delete the successor instead (which has ≤1 child by construction). "Hoist" = transfer
  *ownership* of the key allocation — get this wrong and you get two nodes both believing they own
  the same key (→ double free at `rb_destroy` time).
- Every deletion funnels down to: **what happens when the physically unlinked node is black?**
  → creates a "doubly black" deficit — an **accounting fiction**, not a third color in the enum.
  The empty slot "owes" one black; fixup's job is paying that debt off by climbing toward the root.
- Deletion fixup case families (mirror images exist for all — don't forget them):
  - Sibling is black with no red children → recolor sibling red, debt moves up one level (if
    parent absorbs it by being red → turns black, done, no pointers moved — the "cheap" case,
    deletion's mirror of the red-uncle insert case).
  - Sibling has a red child → rotation drags that red across to the deficient side.
  - Sibling itself is red → rotate first just to reach a shape you already know how to handle.
  - Debt reaching the root just dissolves there (every path lost the same one black — equality
## Milestones (M0–M3 + optional Reach)

| Milestone | What | Est. hours |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Setup: repo, `CLAUDE.md`, toolchain | 1 |
| M1 | Skeleton, insert (+rebalance), find, foreach, validate | 3–4 |
| M2 | Delete (all fixup cases) + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops), green under asan+memcheck | 3–4 |
| M3 | Hardening, edge cases, final clean sweep | 1–2 |
| The Reach (ungraded) | Teardown *without recursion* — O(1) aux space via right-spine trick | 1–2 |
| — | Process artifacts (CLAUDE.md, PROMPTLOG.md, REFLECTION.md), written throughout | 1 |

**Discipline point emphasized repeatedly:** don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust
yet — "less a milestone than an archaeological dig."

### Required operations & testing bar
- Required: `rb_create`, `rb_insert` (w/ rebalancing), `rb_find`, `rb_delete` (full fixup, all
  cases), `rb_size`, `rb_foreach` (in-order), `rb_validate`, `rb_destroy`.
- `rb_validate` must check all 5 invariants + that `rb_size` matches actual node count.
- **Fuzzer:** ≥ 10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops vs. a reference model (sorted array or linked
  list is fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, under both asan and memcheck.
- **Targeted deletion tests are required in addition to fuzzing** (fuzzing alone won't reliably hit
  rare fixup shapes): minimum a red leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a two-children node,
  root deletion — **plus the black-node-with-one-red-child case** the spec adds explicitly. Each
  test must assert `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward.
- **Recursion is allowed** in `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` *for this assignment only* — the next
  assignment revokes it (stack-limited kernel-style constraints).
- **Tip explicitly recommended:** route all allocation through 4-line wrapper functions
  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` (just forwarding to malloc/free for now) — this is the "seam" the *next*
  assignment's fault-injection harness will need. Install now, "while the house is small."

## Toolchain / verification requirements

| Component | Method | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Core tree (insert/find/foreach/validate) | Unit tests + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops) under asan+memcheck | 1.5 |
| Deletion, all fixup cases | Table-driven case tests + fuzzer w/ deletes green | 1.5 |
| Code quality & memory cleanliness | Clean build, zero sanitizer/valgrind findings, sane structure | 1.0 |
| **Program correctness subtotal** | | **4.0** |
| Prompt analysis (transcripts) | TA review for genuine iterative use, corroborated vs. repo | 0.5 |
| Quiz (live walkthrough, on your own code) | Short quiz generated from your submitted code | 0.5 |
3. **Plan mode** (Shift+Tab) for every milestone — agent can read/analyze but not edit. Argue with
   the plan before approving; a plan accepted unmodified on first try is flagged as a red flag.
4. Tests first, then the smallest implementation slice — reject any diff that's too big ("one case
   only").
5. Close the loop with tool evidence — never accept "should pass now"; feed real tool output back.
6. Manage context: `/clear` between milestones, `/compact` mid-task when a debugging thread gets
   noisy. Rule of thumb: new milestone → new session.
7. **Adversarial review in a fresh context** before each milestone commit (`/code-review` skill or
   manually `/clear` + hostile-reviewer prompt) — hunts specifically for use-after-free in successor
   splice, leaked key copy on overwrite, unchecked NULL, missed subtrees in `rb_destroy`.
8. Git discipline — commit at every green state, conversationally directing the agent to do so
   *after you've read the diff*.
9. (Optional) Automate the battery as a slash command (`.claude/commands/battery.md`).

## Practical logistics

# M2 plan: `rb_delete` (all fixup cases) + fuzzer with deletes

## Context

M1 is functionally done (insert with full fixup, find, validate, destroy) and green
under ASan/UBSan. Today's hostile review found and fixed one double free (same-pointer
overwrite). Thirteen delete tests now sit red in `tests/test_rbtree.c` — 11 table cases
plus only-node-then-reuse plus absent-key — all failing for the same reason: `rb_delete`
is the M0 stub returning −1.

M2 per the spec (`Homeworks/hw1/spec-notes.md`): delete with **all** fixup cases, plus a
fuzzer of ≥10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops against a reference model with
`rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, green under ASan **and** valgrind. Two things the
spec fixes for us, so they are not open questions:

- **Two children → "hoist."** Move the successor's key+value into the doomed node's slot,
  then delete the successor (which has ≤1 child). The spec names the bug this is
  guarding against: two nodes that both think they own one key → double free at destroy.
- **No recursion in delete.** Only `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` get the recursion exemption.
  Delete and its fixup are loops.

One M1 leftover matters here: `rb_foreach` is still a stub. The fuzzer's strongest check
("does the tree contain exactly what the model contains, in order?") needs it, and it is
~12 lines. It goes first.

Repo rules that shape every step (`CLAUDE.md` in the repo): never touch `rbtree.h`;
smallest diff that passes; tests before code; goto-cleanup for multi-alloc functions
(delete allocates nothing, so N/A); commit only from green; every non-obvious loop gets
a one-line invariant comment.

---

## The design (what gets built, and why this shape)

All of it lives in `src/rbtree.c`, between `rb_find` and `rb_size`, kept apart from the
insert machinery so a failing delete test points at one function. Names follow the
how-to's suggested map: `tree_minimum`, `transplant`, `delete_fixup`.

### 1. Missing children stay `NULL`; the fixup takes `x_parent` separately

`is_red()` already treats NULL as black, and every existing function assumes NULL
children. CLRS uses a sentinel NIL node so the fixup's `x` always has a parent pointer.
We will **not** add a sentinel: it would touch insert, find, validate, destroy and both
rotations — a large diff to code that is currently trusted, exactly what the spec warns
against ("don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust"). The cost is that
`delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)` needs the parent passed in, because `x` may be NULL.

### 2. Hoist by **swapping** key/value pointers, not copying

When `z` has two children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)`; swap `z->key ↔ y->key` and
`z->value ↔ y->value`; then set `z = y` and carry on as if deleting `y`. Colors do not
move — the tree's shape and coloring are untouched, only the payload moved.

Why swap rather than copy: after a swap, exactly one node owns each key and each value
at every moment, and the node that finally goes through `node_release` is holding the
*doomed* key and value. No new ownership rule, no allocation, no free outside
`node_release`. This also makes the classic "what if the successor is z's own right
child?" question a non-case: we never re-link the successor node, we only empty it and
then delete it where it stands.

### 3. Every delete funnels into "remove a node with ≤1 child"

```
z = node_find(t, key);              if NULL -> return -1 (nothing touched)
if (z->left && z->right)            two children: hoist, then z = successor
x        = z->left ? z->left : z->right     (may be NULL)
x_parent = z->parent
transplant(t, z, x)                 x takes z's place; updates t->root if z was root
need_fixup = (z->color == RB_BLACK) read BEFORE release
node_release(t, z); t->count--;     z is unlinked; nothing in the tree points at it
if (need_fixup) delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)
return 0
```

Release happens before the fixup on purpose: `z` is already unreachable, `x` and
`x_parent` are never `z`, so there is nothing for the fixup to use-after-free — and if
it ever did, ASan would say so immediately instead of at destroy time.

`node_find` is the search loop `rb_find` already has, returning the node instead of the
value. `rb_find` becomes a 3-line wrapper around it. That is the only touch to existing
code; the alternative is duplicating the loop.

### 4. `delete_fixup` — the doubly-black loop (CLRS 13.4 with NULL-as-black)

```
while (x != t->root && !is_red(x)) {          x is "doubly black"; NULL counts as black
    if (x == x_parent->left) {
        w = x_parent->right;                  sibling; never NULL (see below)
        case 1: w red        -> w black, parent red, rotate_left(parent), w = new sibling
        case 2: w's kids both black -> w red; x = x_parent; x_parent = x->parent   (climb)
        case 3: w's near kid red, far kid black -> near kid black, w red,
                                                   rotate_right(w), w = new sibling
        case 4: w's far kid red -> w takes parent's color; parent black; far kid black;
                                   rotate_left(parent); x = t->root  (done)
    } else { mirror: every left/right swapped }
}
if (x != NULL) x->color = RB_BLACK;
```

Facts to be able to say out loud at the walkthrough (they go in the comments):
- **Why `w` is never NULL:** `x` is one black short. Before the delete both of
  `x_parent`'s sides had equal black-height; the removed node was black, so the sibling
  side still has black-height ≥ 2, which needs at least one real node. So `w` exists,
  and in cases 3/4 the "red kid" is red hence non-NULL.
- **Why it terminates:** case 2 climbs (at most height steps). Case 1 always falls into
  2/3/4 with a black sibling, and if it falls into 2 the new `x` is the parent we just
  painted red, so the loop exits on the next test. Cases 3→4 and 4 end it. At most 3
  rotations total.
- **Why "black with one red child" needs no loop:** `x` is red, the loop condition is
  false, and the final line paints `x` black. The debt is paid by the recolor.
- **Root:** transplant already moved `t->root`. Debt reaching the root just dissolves
  (`x == t->root` ends the loop) — every path lost the same one black.
- **Rotations:** reuse `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` unchanged; they already own the
  `t->root` update.

---

## Steps — one slice at a time, each: tests red → smallest code → real output → your commit

Each step ends with `make test` and `make asan` output shown, and the exact commit
command handed to you (git is your call each time). The expected test flips are stated so
we can tell immediately if a slice did more or less than intended.

### Step 0 — `rb_foreach` (M1 leftover, ~12 lines)
- Test first: insert scrambled keys, collect via callback into an array, compare to the
  sorted order; empty tree calls nothing; `ctx` round-trips. Add to `test_rbtree.c`.
- Code: recursive in-order helper (`foreach_subtree`), same shape as `destroy_subtree`.
  Comment: the callback must not insert/delete on the tree it is walking.
- Expect: new test green; the 13 delete tests still red.

### Step 1 — delete for nodes with ≤1 child (no fixup loop yet)
- Add `node_find`, `transplant`, and `rb_delete` as in §3 but with `if (z->left &&
  z->right) return -1;` as a placeholder, and instead of `delete_fixup` just `if
  (is_red(x)) x->color = RB_BLACK;`.
- Expect **8 of 13 flip green:** `red_leaf_*` (2), `black_one_red_child_*` (2),
  `root_one_*_child` (2), `only_node`, `absent`. Still red: `two_children_*` (2),
  `root_two_children`, and `black_leaf_red_sibling_*` (2) — the last two now failing with
  **validate code 7**, not −1, which is the honest state: the node is gone, the debt is unpaid.

### Step 2 — two children: `tree_minimum` + hoist swap
- Tests first — two rows the current table lacks (shapes to be confirmed with the
  scratch dump tool before writing, as today):
  - `two_children_deep_successor`: insert d,b,f,a,c,e,g; delete **d** (successor `e` is two
    levels down, and this is also the root).
  - `two_children_successor_has_child`: insert b,a,d,c,e,f; delete **d** (successor `e`
    has a red right child `f` — the one-child splice happens *inside* the reduction).
  - Both existing `two_children_*` rows already cover "successor is z's own right child".
- Code: replace the placeholder with the hoist.
- Expect: **+5 green** (the 3 old rows + 2 new). Only `black_leaf_red_sibling_*` remain red.

### Step 3 — `delete_fixup`, one case family per slice, mirrors written *with* each case
The harness needs one small generalization first: `struct del_case` takes a **list of
victims** deleted in order (checks run after every one) instead of a single victim. Some
fixup shapes are only reachable after a preparatory red-leaf delete, and this is also what
the drain tests below need.

- **3a — case 2 (black sibling, no red children).** Rows: insert b,a,c,d → delete d then
  **a** (parent is the black root: it absorbs the debt); mirror c,d,b,a → a then **d**.
  Plus the "cheap" variant where a red parent absorbs it: b,a,d,c,e,f → f then **c**;
  mirror e,f,c,d,b,a → a then **d**. Code: the loop skeleton + case 2 + mirror.
- **3b — case 1 (red sibling).** Code: case 1 + mirror. Expect the two
  `black_leaf_red_sibling_*` rows to flip (they go case 1 → case 2 → done).
- **3c — cases 3 and 4 (sibling has a red child).** Rows: near-red b,a,d,c → delete
  **a**; mirror c,d,a,b → **d**. Far-red b,a,c,d → **a**; mirror c,d,b,a → **d**.
  Code: cases 3 and 4 + mirrors.
- **3d — drain tests.** Insert d,b,f,a,c,e,g and delete all seven in insertion order, in
  reverse, and in sorted order, validating after every delete, ending at size 0 with all
  seven values freed and 0 live blocks. These hit multi-level climbs the single-victim
  rows cannot.
- Expect after 3d: **the whole table green**, 0 leaks.

### Step 4 — fuzzer with deletes (`tests/fuzz.c`)
- Reference model: a flag-array indexed by key number (`present[k]`, `expect_val[k]`)
  over a small key space (~512 keys, so deletes and overwrites actually hit). Simpler and
  more obviously correct than the spec's "sorted array" suggestion; it *is* sorted by
  construction.
- Ops (fixed seed, printed on failure; op count = `argv[1]`, optional seed = `argv[2]`):
  insert with a fresh malloc'd value (tree owns it, `value_free = free`), find (compare
  pointer to model), delete (compare return code to model presence). Every 100 ops:
  `rb_validate == 0`, `rb_size == model count`, and `rb_foreach` output equals the model's
  in-order key list. At the end: destroy, `rb_debug_live_allocs == 0`.
- On any mismatch: print op number, seed, and the op, exit 1 — so a failure can be
  shrunk to a short repro before we debug it.
- `make test` already runs it at 10⁵ ops; `make memcheck` at 2×10⁴.

### Step 5 — full battery, valgrind, hostile review, docs
- `make test` and `make asan` here. **`make memcheck` cannot run on this Mac** (no valgrind
  on Apple Silicon) — it needs a Linux machine (Docker `ubuntu` + `apt install valgrind
  gcc make`, or a school Linux box). This is a real gap to close before calling M2 done;
  the repo's CLAUDE.md already says never to report memcheck as passing here.
- Fresh-context hostile review of the M2 diff, hunting the spec's named families:
  use-after-free in the successor hoist, key ownership after the swap, unchecked NULL,
  the mirror cases, `rb_destroy` after many deletes.
- Docs: README milestone changelog, repo CLAUDE.md status + code map (add
  `node_find`/`tree_minimum`/`transplant`/`delete_fixup`), PROMPTLOG episode for this plan
  and whatever you change in it, DEVLOG.

---

## Argue with this (the spec wants you to)

1. **Swap vs. CLRS node transplant.** Swap is smaller and makes ownership trivially right.
   Transplant preserves node identity, which nothing in this API needs.
2. **NULL + `x_parent` vs. a sentinel NIL.** Sentinel makes the fixup prettier at the cost
   of rewriting trusted code.
3. **`node_find` shared with `rb_find`** (3-line touch to existing code) vs. duplicating
   the search loop.
4. **Fixup slice order 2 → 1 → 3/4** vs. writing the whole loop at once.
5. **Releasing `z` before the fixup** vs. after.
6. **Flag-array model** vs. an actual sorted array in the fuzzer.
7. **`rb_foreach` first** vs. deferring it and having the fuzzer check only via `rb_find`.

## Verification (end to end)

- Failing-test count per step: 13 → 13 (step 0) → 5 (step 1) → 2 (step 2) → 0 (step 3).
- `make asan` green after every slice; `make test` runs the fuzzer at 10⁵ ops.
- `make memcheck` on Linux: zero errors, zero leaks, both binaries.
- `rb_debug_live_allocs() == 0` after every test and after the fuzzer.
- Hostile review of the M2 diff finds nothing in the spec's named bug families.

child?" question a non-case: we never re-link the successor node, we only empty it and
then delete it where it stands.

```

if (z->left && z->right)            two children: hoist, then z = successor
x        = z->left ? z->left : z->right     (may be NULL)
x_parent = z->parent
transplant(t, z, x)                 x takes z's place; updates t->root if z was root
need_fixup = (z->color == RB_BLACK) read BEFORE release
node_release(t, z); t->count--;     z is unlinked; nothing in the tree points at it
if (need_fixup) delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)
return 0
```

Release happens before the fixup on purpose: `z` is already unreachable, `x` and
`x_parent` are never `z`, so there is nothing for the fixup to use-after-free — and if
it ever did, ASan would say so immediately instead of at destroy time.

`node_find` is the search loop `rb_find` already has, returning the node instead of the
value. `rb_find` becomes a 3-line wrapper around it. That is the only touch to existing
code; the alternative is duplicating the loop.

while (x != t->root && !is_red(x)) {          x is "doubly black"; NULL counts as black
    if (x == x_parent->left) {
        w = x_parent->right;                  sibling; never NULL (see below)
        case 1: w red        -> w black, parent red, rotate_left(parent), w = new sibling
        case 2: w's kids both black -> w red; x = x_parent; x_parent = x->parent   (climb)
        case 3: w's near kid red, far kid black -> near kid black, w red,
                                                   rotate_right(w), w = new sibling
        case 4: w's far kid red -> w takes parent's color; parent black; far kid black;
                                   rotate_left(parent); x = t->root  (done)
    } else { mirror: every left/right swapped }
}
if (x != NULL) x->color = RB_BLACK;
```

Facts to be able to say out loud at the walkthrough (they go in the comments):
- **Why `w` is never NULL:** `x` is one black short. Before the delete both of
  `x_parent`'s sides had equal black-height; the removed node was black, so the sibling
  side still has black-height ≥ 2, which needs at least one real node. So `w` exists,
  and in cases 3/4 the "red kid" is red hence non-NULL.
- **Why it terminates:** case 2 climbs (at most height steps). Case 1 always falls into
  2/3/4 with a black sibling, and if it falls into 2 the new `x` is the parent we just
  painted red, so the loop exits on the next test. Cases 3→4 and 4 end it. At most 3
  rotations total.
- **Why "black with one red child" needs no loop:** `x` is red, the loop condition is
  false, and the final line paints `x` black. The debt is paid by the recolor.
- **Root:** transplant already moved `t->root`. Debt reaching the root just dissolves
  (`x == t->root` ends the loop) — every path lost the same one black.
- **Rotations:** reuse `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` unchanged; they already own the

Here are the seven, each with what I'd pick, the other option, and why. No code until you've decided.

**1. Two-children deletion: swap the key/value pointers with the successor, vs. CLRS-style node transplant**

- *My pick:* swap. Find the successor, exchange `key` and `value` pointers between the doomed node and the successor node, then delete the successor node where it stands. Colors and shape don't move; only the payload does.
- *Alternative:* CLRS "transplant" — physically unlink the successor node and re-link it into the doomed node's position, copying the doomed node's color onto it. Has a special case when the successor is the doomed node's direct right child.
- *Why swap:* at every moment exactly one node owns each key and value, so `node_release` frees the right things with no new ownership rule. No allocation, no special case for "successor is my own right child." The spec itself says "hoist," and its named failure mode (two nodes thinking they own one key) is exactly what the swap makes impossible. Transplant's one advantage — node identity survives — is worthless here because nothing in the API ever hands out a node.

**2. Missing children stay `NULL` (fixup takes `x_parent` as a separate argument), vs. a sentinel NIL node**

- *My pick:* keep `NULL`. The fixup signature becomes `delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)` because `x` can be `NULL` and a `NULL` has no parent pointer.
- *Alternative:* one shared black sentinel node that every "missing child" points to. Then `x` is always a real node with a parent, and the fixup reads like the textbook.
- *Why NULL:* `is_red()` already treats `NULL` as black, and insert, find, validate, destroy, and both rotations all assume `NULL` children. A sentinel means rewriting trusted, tested code — the spec's warning about "debugging delete on top of an insert you don't trust" applies directly. The extra argument is the whole cost.

**3. One shared `node_find` used by both `rb_find` and `rb_delete`, vs. duplicating the search loop**

- *My pick:* add `static node_find()` returning the node; `rb_find` becomes a 3-line wrapper around it.
- *Alternative:* copy the 7-line search loop into `rb_delete` and leave `rb_find` untouched — zero risk to existing code.
- *Why share:* one search loop means one place for a comparison bug to live. The touch to `rb_find` is tiny and the existing find tests cover it. Against it: the repo rule "don't refactor unrelated code" — I'd argue the search is *related*, but it's a fair call either way.

**4. Build the fixup one case family per slice (case 2 → case 1 → cases 3/4), vs. writing the whole loop at once**

- *My pick:* slices, mirrors written with each case, tests for that case first.
- *Alternative:* write all four cases plus mirrors in one go, then make the table green.
- *Why slices:* each slice flips a known set of tests, so if something unexpected goes green or red we know which case did it. Case 2 goes first because case 1 always falls *into* case 2/3/4 — it can't be tested alone. Against it: more commits, more ceremony, for ~50 lines of code.

**5. Free the doomed node before running the fixup, vs. after**

- *My pick:* before. Unlink it, read its color into a local, release it, then fix up.
- *Alternative:* fix up first, release last — the textbook order.
- *Why before:* once the node is unlinked nothing in the tree points at it, and the fixup only touches `x` and `x_parent`, neither of which is the freed node. Freeing first means that if the fixup ever *did* touch it, ASan reports it at that exact line instead of as a confusing double-free at destroy. Against it: if you'd find the textbook order easier to explain at the walkthrough, that's a legitimate reason to keep it.

**6. Fuzzer reference model: a flag array indexed by key number, vs. an actual sorted array**

- *My pick:* fixed key space of ~512 keys (`k0000`…`k0511`), and the model is `present[k]` + `expected_value[k]`. Walking 0…511 *is* sorted order, so the in-order comparison is a plain loop.
- *Alternative:* a real sorted array of strings with insertion/removal by shifting, as the spec suggests.
- *Why flag array:* it's too simple to be wrong, which is the whole point of a reference model. A small key space also means deletes and overwrites actually hit existing keys often instead of mostly missing. Against it: the spec literally says "sorted array or linked list"; the flag array is a sorted array in spirit, but if you'd rather match the wording exactly, that's cheap too.

**7. Do `rb_foreach` first (step 0), vs. deferring it and letting the fuzzer check contents only through `rb_find`**

- *My pick:* first. It's an M1 leftover, ~12 lines, recursive like `destroy_subtree`, and it gives the fuzzer its strongest check: "the tree contains exactly the model's keys, in order."
- *Alternative:* leave it for later; the fuzzer checks `rb_size`, `rb_validate`, and `rb_find` per key, which is nearly as strong.
- *Why first:* it closes M1 properly (the repo's CLAUDE.md still lists it as "next"), and `rb_validate` already proves ordering, so `foreach` mostly proves *traversal* — but a traversal bug is exactly the kind that only shows up under volume.

Take your time with these.

input.plan:
# M2 plan: `rb_delete` (all fixup cases) + fuzzer with deletes

## Context

M1 is functionally done (insert with full fixup, find, validate, destroy) and green
under ASan/UBSan. Today's hostile review found and fixed one double free (same-pointer
overwrite). Thirteen delete tests now sit red in `tests/test_rbtree.c` — 11 table cases
plus only-node-then-reuse plus absent-key — all failing for the same reason: `rb_delete`
is the M0 stub returning −1.

M2 per the spec (`Homeworks/hw1/spec-notes.md`): delete with **all** fixup cases, plus a
fuzzer of ≥10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops against a reference model with
`rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, green under ASan **and** valgrind. Two things the
spec fixes for us, so they are not open questions:

- **Two children → "hoist."** Move the successor's key+value into the doomed node's slot,
  then delete the successor (which has ≤1 child). The spec names the bug this is
  guarding against: two nodes that both think they own one key → double free at destroy.
- **No recursion in delete.** Only `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` get the recursion exemption.
  Delete and its fixup are loops.

One M1 leftover matters here: `rb_foreach` is still a stub. The fuzzer's strongest check
("does the tree contain exactly what the model contains, in order?") needs it, and it is
~12 lines. It goes first.

Repo rules that shape every step (`CLAUDE.md` in the repo): never touch `rbtree.h`;
smallest diff that passes; tests before code; goto-cleanup for multi-alloc functions
(delete allocates nothing, so N/A); commit only from green; every non-obvious loop gets
a one-line invariant comment.

---

## The design (what gets built, and why this shape)

All of it lives in `src/rbtree.c`, between `rb_find` and `rb_size`, kept apart from the
insert machinery so a failing delete test points at one function. Names follow the
how-to's suggested map: `tree_minimum`, `transplant`, `delete_fixup`.

### 1. Missing children stay `NULL`; the fixup takes `x_parent` separately

`is_red()` already treats NULL as black, and every existing function assumes NULL
children. CLRS uses a sentinel NIL node so the fixup's `x` always has a parent pointer.
We will **not** add a sentinel: it would touch insert, find, validate, destroy and both
rotations — a large diff to code that is currently trusted, exactly what the spec warns
against ("don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust"). The cost is that
`delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)` needs the parent passed in, because `x` may be NULL.

### 2. Hoist by **swapping** key/value pointers, not copying

When `z` has two children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)`; swap `z->key ↔ y->key` and
`z->value ↔ y->value`; then set `z = y` and carry on as if deleting `y`. Colors do not
move — the tree's shape and coloring are untouched, only the payload moved.

Why swap rather than copy: after a swap, exactly one node owns each key and each value
at every moment, and the node that finally goes through `node_release` is holding the
*doomed* key and value. No new ownership rule, no allocation, no free outside
`node_release`. This also makes the classic "what if the successor is z's own right
child?" question a non-case: we never re-link the successor node, we only empty it and
then delete it where it stands.

### 3. Every delete funnels into "remove a node with ≤1 child"

```
z = node_find(t, key);              if NULL -> return -1 (nothing touched)
if (z->left && z->right)            two children: hoist, then z = successor
x        = z->left ? z->left : z->right     (may be NULL)
x_parent = z->parent
transplant(t, z, x)                 x takes z's place; updates t->root if z was root
need_fixup = (z->color == RB_BLACK) read BEFORE release
node_release(t, z); t->count--;     z is unlinked; nothing in the tree points at it
if (need_fixup) delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)
return 0
```

Release happens before the fixup on purpose: `z` is already unreachable, `x` and
`x_parent` are never `z`, so there is nothing for the fixup to use-after-free — and if
it ever did, ASan would say so immediately instead of at destroy time.

**Decided (Nick):** `rb_find` is not touched. The search loop is written inline at the top
of `rb_delete` — same loop, stops at the node instead of returning the value. Existing
code stays exactly as it is.

### 4. `delete_fixup` — the doubly-black loop (CLRS 13.4 with NULL-as-black)

```
while (x != t->root && !is_red(x)) {          x is "doubly black"; NULL counts as black
    if (x == x_parent->left) {
        w = x_parent->right;                  sibling; never NULL (see below)
        case 1: w red        -> w black, parent red, rotate_left(parent), w = new sibling
        case 2: w's kids both black -> w red; x = x_parent; x_parent = x->parent   (climb)
        case 3: w's near kid red, far kid black -> near kid black, w red,
                                                   rotate_right(w), w = new sibling
        case 4: w's far kid red -> w takes parent's color; parent black; far kid black;
                                   rotate_left(parent); x = t->root  (done)
    } else { mirror: every left/right swapped }
}
if (x != NULL) x->color = RB_BLACK;
```

Facts to be able to say out loud at the walkthrough (they go in the comments):
- **Why `w` is never NULL:** `x` is one black short. Before the delete both of
  `x_parent`'s sides had equal black-height; the removed node was black, so the sibling
  side still has black-height ≥ 2, which needs at least one real node. So `w` exists,
  and in cases 3/4 the "red kid" is red hence non-NULL.
- **Why it terminates:** case 2 climbs (at most height steps). Case 1 always falls into
  2/3/4 with a black sibling, and if it falls into 2 the new `x` is the parent we just
  painted red, so the loop exits on the next test. Cases 3→4 and 4 end it. At most 3
  rotations total.
- **Why "black with one red child" needs no loop:** `x` is red, the loop condition is

Done. Here's the full picture, top to bottom, with where each piece lives.

## How a delete flows

**[rb_delete:467](src/rbtree.c:467)** — four moves, in order:

1. **Find the node** ([471](src/rbtree.c:471)) — the same walk `rb_find` does, but it stops at the node. Absent → `-1`, nothing touched.
2. **Two children? Hoist** ([484](src/rbtree.c:484)) — `tree_minimum(z->right)` finds the successor `y`. Swap the `key` and `value` *pointers* between `z` and `y`. Now `z`'s slot holds the successor's payload (still in order), and `y`'s node holds the doomed payload. Set `z = y`. Colors and shape never moved.
3. **Splice out** ([500](src/rbtree.c:500)) — `z` now has ≤1 child, `x`. Remember `z`'s color, `transplant` makes `z`'s parent point at `x` (and moves `t->root` if `z` was the root), then `node_release(z)` frees the doomed key, value, and node. Count goes down.
4. **Fix up only if `z` was black** ([509](src/rbtree.c:509)) — removing a red node cost nothing. Removing a black one left every path through `x` one black short.

**[delete_fixup:389](src/rbtree.c:389)** — the loop runs while `x` is "doubly black" (black or `NULL`, and not the root). Each pass looks at the sibling `w`:

- **Case 1** ([396](src/rbtree.c:396)) — `w` is red. Rotate at the parent so `x` gets a black sibling. Fall through.
- **Case 2** ([405](src/rbtree.c:405)) — `w` is black with no red child. Paint `w` red so both sides are short by one; the debt moves up to the parent. If the parent is red, the loop exits and the last line paints it black — debt paid. If it's the root, the debt dissolves.
- **Case 3** ([413](src/rbtree.c:413)) — `w` has a red child on the *near* side only. Rotate at `w` to move it to the far side. Fall into 4.
- **Case 4** ([420](src/rbtree.c:420)) — `w` has a red child on the *far* side. Rotate at the parent, recolor. Debt paid, loop ends.
- **Mirror** ([431](src/rbtree.c:431)) — the same four with every left/right swapped.

Two things worth being able to say cold at the walkthrough, both in the header comment: why `w` is never `NULL` (the sibling side kept black-height ≥ 2 when a black came off `x`'s side), and why `x == x_parent->left` picks the right side even when `x` is `NULL` (only the emptied side can be `NULL`).

- `make test` / `make asan`: **all 13 red checks flipped green in one go**, 0 leaks.
- Scratch exhaustive run: every insertion order of ≤7 keys × every single delete × three full drains — 161,276 deletes, 0 failures, 0 leaks under ASan. That covers cases 2/3/4 and mirrors, which the 13 project tests don't yet reach (that's plan step 3, when you say so).

Working tree vs `HEAD`: `src/rbtree.c` (+192: the guard and the delete section), `tests/test_rbtree.c` (+254), `.gitignore` (−1), plus `PROMPTLOG.md` (+13 — yours, I didn't touch it), and `transcripts/` untracked. git add src/rbtree.c tests/test_rbtree.c .gitignore transcripts/ PROMPTLOG.md && git commit -m "M2: rb_delete with full fixup; table-driven delete tests; same-pointer overwrite guard"
```

# rbtree-lab: project rules

## Commands
- Build & unit tests: `make test`
- Sanitizers: `make asan`   Valgrind: `make memcheck`
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.

## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
  leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
  looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.

## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.

## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
  approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".

## Code map
- `src/rbtree.c` — the whole implementation. Opaque `struct rbtree` and the
  node struct live here, invisible to tests.
- All allocation goes through `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` in that file, never
  malloc/free directly. That seam is what HW2 swaps out.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit and table-driven case tests.
- `tests/fuzz.c` — random ops vs. a reference model; op count is `argv[1]`.

## Ownership
Three separately-owned things per node: the node, the tree's private key
copy, and the caller's `void *value`.
- rb_insert returns 0 -> tree owns value. Returns -1 -> caller still owns it.
- Overwrite frees the OLD value via value_free first.
- Rotations change topology only, never ownership.

## Environment
`make memcheck` cannot run on this Mac: no valgrind on Apple Silicon, and
ASan on macOS has no LeakSanitizer. Leak checking needs a Linux machine.
Never report memcheck as passing here.

## Status
M1 steps 1-10 done: full red-black insert. rotate_left/rotate_right own the
t->root update. insert_fixup handles red-uncle (recolor+climb) and
black-uncle (1-2 rotations) with mirrors. rb_validate checks all 5 rules +
parent links + count; failure codes 1-7 name the broken rule.
Still stubs: rb_foreach (M1), rb_delete (M2). Fuzzer is a stub.
Next: rb_foreach (in-order, recursive), then the fuzzer (inserts/finds vs a
sorted-array reference model, validate every 100 ops).

## What's in slice 1 ([src/rbtree.c:328](src/rbtree.c:328)–[420](src/rbtree.c:420))

Three pieces, about 60 lines without comments:

- **`tree_minimum`** ([341](src/rbtree.c:341)) — walk left until you can't. Finds the successor.
- **`transplant`** ([353](src/rbtree.c:353)) — "make `u`'s parent point at `v` instead." Three-way branch (root / left child / right child), then set `v->parent` if `v` exists. This is the only place a node is unlinked.
- **`rb_delete`** ([367](src/rbtree.c:367)):
  1. find the node, or `-1`
  2. two children → swap key/value pointers with the successor, then aim at the successor's node instead (it has ≤1 child by construction)
  3. read the color, `transplant`, `node_release`, count down
  4. if the removed node was black and had one child, paint that child black — done. If it was black with *no* child, do nothing yet: that's the loop.

What's green tells you the ownership story is right: every two-children row frees exactly one value (the doomed one, not the successor's), and every survivor still answers with its original pointer.

content.text:
**Table green: 13/13**, `make test` and `make asan` both clean, 0 leaks. The scratch exhaustive run (every tree of ≤7 nodes, 161,276 deletes) is also 0 failures under ASan, which is where cases 2, 3, 4 and their mirrors actually get exercised until the step-3 rows exist.

## What this slice added (+~95 lines, all in one function)

**`delete_fixup`** at [src/rbtree.c:389](src/rbtree.c:389). The loop runs while `x` is doubly black — black or `NULL`, and not the root. Each pass looks at the sibling `w` and does one of:

- **Case 1** ([396](src/rbtree.c:396)) — `w` red → rotate at the parent so `x` gets a black sibling, fall through.
- **Case 2** ([405](src/rbtree.c:405)) — `w` black, no red child → paint `w` red; the debt moves up to the parent. Red parent absorbs it (loop exits, last line paints it black). Root dissolves it.
- **Case 3** ([413](src/rbtree.c:413)) — `w`'s red child is on the *near* side → rotate at `w` to push it to the far side, fall into 4.
- **Case 4** ([420](src/rbtree.c:420)) — `w`'s red child is on the *far* side → rotate at the parent, recolor. Paid, loop ends.
- **Mirror** ([431](src/rbtree.c:431)) — same four, left/right swapped.

And two lines in `rb_delete`: `x_parent = z->parent` captured before `z` is freed, and the slice-1 "one red child" special case replaced by the call — a red `x` fails the loop test on entry and the last line paints it black, so the special case is now just the loop's shortest path.

The two things to be able to explain cold are in the header comment: why `w` can never be `NULL` (the sibling side kept black-height ≥ 2 when a black came off `x`'s side), and why `x == x_parent->left` picks the right side even when `x` is `NULL` (only the emptied side can be `NULL`).

Three things, in order: the workflow, the table rows (shapes confirmed first), then `CLAUDE.md`.

## 1. GitHub Actions workflow

One design point worth knowing: the Makefile's `memcheck` target depends on `all`, and `all` won't rebuild if `build/` is already up to date. So if `make asan` runs *before* `make memcheck`, valgrind gets the sanitizer binaries — and valgrind and ASan can't coexist (ASan's shadow memory fails under valgrind). The workflow orders the steps `test → memcheck → asan` to avoid that; `asan` cleans first anyway. Also, Ubuntu 24.04's default gcc is 13, whose C23 flag is spelled `-std=c2x`; `gcc-14` accepts `-std=c23` as the Makefile is written, so the workflow installs that and passes `CC=gcc-14`.

# rbtree-lab: project rules

## Commands
- Build & unit tests: `make test`
- Sanitizers: `make asan`   Valgrind: `make memcheck`
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.

## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
  leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
  looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.

## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.

## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
  approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".

## Code map
- `src/rbtree.c` — the whole implementation. Opaque `struct rbtree` and the
  node struct live here, invisible to tests.
- All allocation goes through `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` in that file, never
  malloc/free directly. That seam is what HW2 swaps out.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit and table-driven case tests.
- `tests/fuzz.c` — random ops vs. a reference model; op count is `argv[1]`.

## Ownership
Three separately-owned things per node: the node, the tree's private key
copy, and the caller's `void *value`.
- rb_insert returns 0 -> tree owns value. Returns -1 -> caller still owns it.
- Overwrite frees the OLD value via value_free first.
- Rotations change topology only, never ownership.

## Environment
`make memcheck` cannot run on this Mac: no valgrind on Apple Silicon, and
ASan on macOS has no LeakSanitizer. Leak checking needs a Linux machine.
Never report memcheck as passing here.

## Status
M1 steps 1-10 done: full red-black insert. rotate_left/rotate_right own the
t->root update. insert_fixup handles red-uncle (recolor+climb) and
black-uncle (1-2 rotations) with mirrors. rb_validate checks all 5 rules +
parent links + count; failure codes 1-7 name the broken rule.
Still stubs: rb_foreach (M1), rb_delete (M2). Fuzzer is a stub.
Next: rb_foreach (in-order, recursive), then the fuzzer (inserts/finds vs a
sorted-array reference model, validate every 100 ops).

# rbtree-lab: project rules

## Commands
- Build & unit tests: `make test`
- Sanitizers: `make asan`   Valgrind: `make memcheck` (Linux only, see Environment)
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.
- Fuzzer by hand: `./build/fuzz <ops> [seed]`. A failure prints its seed and
  a reproduce command; rerun with that, then shrink the op count.

## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
  leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
  looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.

## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.

## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
  approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".

## Code map
- `src/rbtree.c` — the whole implementation. Opaque `struct rbtree` and the
  node struct live here, invisible to tests. Missing children are NULL (no
  sentinel); `is_red` treats NULL as black.
  - `node_alloc`/`node_release` — the only place a node's two allocations are
    made and freed.
  - `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` — shape only; they own the `t->root` update.
  - `insert_fixup` — red-uncle recolor+climb, black-uncle 1-2 rotations.
  - `tree_minimum`, `transplant`, `delete_fixup`, `rb_delete` — deletion,
    kept apart from insert. Two children: swap key/value pointers with the
    successor, then delete the successor's node. `delete_fixup(t, x, x_parent)`
    takes the parent separately because x may be NULL. No recursion in delete.
  - `validate_subtree`, `destroy_subtree`, `foreach_subtree` — recursive;
    allowed for this assignment only.
- All allocation goes through `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` in that file, never
  malloc/free directly. That seam is what HW2 swaps out. `rb_debug_live_allocs`
  (not in the header; tests declare it) counts live blocks for leak checks.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit tests plus the table-driven delete cases: each
  row is an insertion string (fixes the shape) and a deletion string; checks
  run after every delete. Shapes in the comments were dumped, not guessed.
- `tests/fuzz.c` — random insert/find/delete vs. a flag-array model over 512
  keys, own xorshift PRNG (same seed = same ops on every machine),
  rb_validate + full in-order comparison every 100 ops. `argv[1]` ops,
  optional `argv[2]` seed.
- `.github/workflows/battery.yml` — test, memcheck, asan on Ubuntu on every
  push. Order matters there: memcheck before asan (valgrind cannot run
  sanitizer binaries, and `make memcheck` does not rebuild).

## Ownership
Three separately-owned things per node: the node, the tree's private key
copy, and the caller's `void *value`.

- Overwrite frees the OLD value via value_free first.
- Rotations change topology only, never ownership.

**[tests/test_rbtree.c](tests/test_rbtree.c)** — the delete table is now **24 rows** ([delete_cases](tests/test_rbtree.c:564)). Each row is an insertion string and a deletion string, checks after every delete. New: 2 harder two-children shapes, case 2 ×4 (root absorbs / red parent absorbs, with mirrors), case 3→4 ×2, case 4 ×2, three full drains. Every shape in the comments — including the intermediate ones after a preparatory delete — came out of the dump tool.
